# What you'll learn

<div class="grid-3">

<div class="card purple">
<span class="label label-purple">1 · WORK SAFELY</span>
<p>Keep your experiments separate from the shared project.</p>
</div>

<div class="card blue">

<p>Review changes together before they go live.</p>
</div>

<div class="card green">

# The problem

## Without a system, teamwork gets messy fast

<div class="grid-2">

<div class="card">
<span class="label label-purple medium">WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE</span>

```text
notebook.ipynb
      ↓
final_model_v7_FINAL.ipynb
      ↓
"which file is the latest?"
```

</div>

<div class="card blue">
<span class="label label-blue">QUESTIONS NOBODY CAN ANSWER</span>
<ul>
<li>Who changed it?</li>
<li>What exactly changed?</li>
<li>Can we review it first?</li>
<li>Can we undo it?</li>
</ul>
</div>

</div>



# Git vs GitHub

## The one distinction to remember

<div class="grid-2">

<div class="card purple">
<span class="label label-purple">GIT</span>
<h3>The tool on your computer</h3>
<ul>
<li>Records every change</li>
<li>Saves checkpoints (commits)</li>
<li>Lets you compare and go back</li>
</ul>
</div>

<div class="card blue">
<span class="label label-blue">GITHUB</span>
<h3>The place your team shares it</h3>
<ul>
<li>Hosts the project online</li>
<li>Pull Requests and reviews</li>
<li>Issues and automated checks</li>
</ul>
</div>

</div>

<div class="note">
<p><strong>Git</strong> tracks the changes. <strong>GitHub</strong> is where the team works together around them.</p>
</div>



# The whole workflow in one picture

<div class="flow">
<span class="node feature medium">Branch</span>
<span class="arrow medium">→</span>
<span class="node medium">Commit</span>
<span class="arrow medium">→</span>
<span class="node medium">Push</span>
<span class="arrow medium">→</span>
<span class="node blue medium">Pull Request</span>
<span class="arrow medium">→</span>
<span class="node green medium">Review + Checks</span>
<span class="arrow medium">→</span>
<span class="node main medium">main</span>
</div>

<div class="note">
<p>The rest of the workshop just walks through this line, one step at a time.</p>
</div>



# Step 1 · Start tracking changes

## Turn a normal folder into a Git project

```bash
git init          # start tracking this folder
git add .         # stage your files
git commit -m "Initial project setup"
```

<div class="note">
<p>A <strong>commit</strong> is a saved checkpoint. You can always come back to it.</p>
</div>



# Write commit messages people understand

<div class="grid-2">

<div class="card">
<span class="label label-purple medium">NOT HELPFUL</span>

```bash
git commit -m "stuff"
```

<p class="muted">Nobody knows what changed.</p>
</div>

<div class="card green">
<span class="label label-green medium">HELPFUL</span>

```bash
git commit -m "Add baseline churn model"
```

<p class="muted">Answers the question: what changed?</p>
</div>

</div>



# Read the history

## Anyone should be able to see what happened

```bash
git log --oneline
```

```text
a91f4d2 Add baseline churn model
31c72a1 Initial project setup
```

Look at a specific change:

```bash
git show a91f4d2
```



# Step 2 · Put it on GitHub

## Send your local project to the shared repository

```bash
git branch -M main

git remote add origin \
  https://github.com/YOUR-ORG/churn-project.git

git push -u origin main
```

<div class="flow">
<span class="node medium">Your computer</span>
<span class="arrow medium">git push →</span>
<span class="node main medium">GitHub · main</span>
</div>



# Three commands you'll use daily

<div class="grid-3">

<div class="card purple">
<span class="label label-purple">FIRST TIME</span>
<h3><code>git clone</code></h3>
<p>Download the repository.</p>
</div>

<div class="card blue">
<span class="label label-blue">GET UPDATES</span>
<h3><code>git pull</code></h3>
<p>Bring in the team's latest changes.</p>
</div>

<div class="card green">
<span class="label label-green">SEND WORK</span>
<h3><code>git push</code></h3>
<p>Upload your commits.</p>
</div>

</div>



# Step 3 · Work on a branch

## Never experiment directly on <code>main</code>

```bash
git switch -c feature/new-model
```

<div class="grid-2">

<div class="card">
<span class="label label-purple">WHY</span>
<p>A branch is a safe copy where you can make changes without touching the shared project.</p>
</div>

<div class="card blue">
<span class="label label-blue">NAMING</span>
<p><code>feature/clean-data</code></p>
<p><code>feature/random-forest</code></p>
<p><code>experiment/xgboost</code></p>
</div>

</div>



# The daily loop on a branch

<div class="steps">
<div class="step medium"><div class="num">1</div><p>Create branch</p></div>
<div class="step medium"><div class="num">2</div><p>Make changes</p></div>
<div class="step medium"><div class="num">3</div><p>Commit</p></div>
<div class="step medium"><div class="num">4</div><p>Push</p></div>
<div class="step medium"><div class="num">5</div><p>Open PR</p></div>
</div>

```bash
git switch -c feature/new-model

git add .
git commit -m "Add baseline model"

git push -u origin feature/new-model
```



# 🧪 Quick check

## Which command makes a new branch AND switches to it?

<div class="grid-2">

<div class="card">
<p><strong>A</strong> &nbsp; <code>git branch feature/model</code></p>
<p><strong>B</strong> &nbsp; <code>git switch -c feature/model</code></p>
</div>

<div class="card">
<p><strong>C</strong> &nbsp; <code>git checkout main</code></p>
<p><strong>D</strong> &nbsp; <code>git push origin main</code></p>
</div>

</div>

<details>
<summary>Reveal answer</summary>
<p><strong class="green-text">B.</strong> It creates the branch and moves you onto it in one step.</p>
</details>



# Step 4 · Pull Requests

## A Pull Request is where the team reviews your change

<div class="flow">
<span class="node feature medium">feature/model</span>
<span class="arrow medium">→ Pull Request →</span>
<span class="node main medium">main</span>
</div>

<div class="grid-3">

<div class="card purple">
<span class="label label-purple">AUTHOR</span>
<p>Explains the change.</p>
</div>

<div class="card blue">
<span class="label label-blue">REVIEWER</span>
<p>Asks questions, suggests fixes.</p>
</div>

<div class="card green">
<span class="label label-green">CHECKS</span>
<p>Run automatically.</p>
</div>

</div>

<div class="note">
<p>The point isn't clicking "merge" — it's the <strong>shared review before the change reaches <code>main</code></strong>.</p>
</div>



# Merge conflicts

## Git can spot a clash. It can't decide who's right.

Two people change the same line:

```python
threshold = 0.50     # yours
threshold = 0.65     # theirs
```

Git shows both and asks you to choose:

```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
threshold = 0.50
=======
threshold = 0.65
>>>>>>> feature/model
```

<div class="note">
<p><strong>You</strong> pick the right value, edit the file, then <code>git add</code> and <code>git commit</code>.</p>
</div>



# Don't commit everything

## Use a <code>.gitignore</code> file

```text
data/
.env
credentials.json
__pycache__/
.ipynb_checkpoints/
```

<div class="grid-2">

<div class="card">
<span class="label label-purple">KEEP OUT</span>
<p>Secrets, large data, and generated files.</p>
</div>

<div class="card green">
<span class="label label-green">REMEMBER</span>
<p>GitHub is for collaboration — not for publishing sensitive data.</p>
</div>

</div>



# A tidy repository

## Structure makes the project easy to pick up

```text
churn-project/
├── data/
├── notebooks/        # explore & visualize
├── src/              # reusable, tested code
│   ├── preprocessing.py
│   └── model.py
├── tests/
├── README.md
├── requirements.txt
└── .gitignore
```

<div class="note">
<p>Explore in <strong>notebooks</strong>, then move stable logic into <strong><code>src/</code></strong>.</p>
</div>



# A README that welcomes new teammates

## Answer these six questions

<div class="grid-2">

<div class="card">
<ul>
<li>What problem are we solving?</li>
<li>How do I install it?</li>
<li>How do I run it?</li>
<li>Where is the data?</li>
<li>How is it structured?</li>
<li>How do I contribute?</li>
</ul>
</div>

<div class="card green">

```markdown
# Customer Churn Prediction

Predict customer churn with ML.

## Setup
pip install -r requirements.txt

## Run
python -m src.model
```

</div>

</div>



# Automated checks (CI)

## What if every Pull Request tested itself?

<div class="flow">
<span class="node feature medium">Pull Request</span>
<span class="arrow medium">→</span>
<span class="node blue medium">GitHub Actions</span>
<span class="arrow medium">→</span>
<span class="node green medium">Tests run</span>
<span class="arrow medium">→</span>
<span class="node main medium">Merge</span>
</div>

A small file turns this on:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/tests.yml
name: Tests
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest
```



# When a check fails

<div class="grid-2">

<div class="card green">
<span class="label label-green">PASS</span>
<p>Keep reviewing and merge when ready.</p>
</div>

<div class="card purple">
<span class="label label-purple">FAIL</span>
<p>Investigate and fix the branch <strong>before</strong> merging.</p>
</div>

</div>

<div class="note">
<p>A failing check is an early warning that something may be broken.</p>
</div>
